title: Are the payoffs measuring the pressure that actually drives choice?
hidden_assumption: The payoff numbers include the consequences the actor actually cares about, and separate actors are not being silently merged into one objective.
why_it_exists: Every solution test reads incentives through payoffs. If reputation, delay, risk, outside options, punishment, or private costs are missing, the model may solve a clean mathematical problem that is not the real strategic problem.
audit_test: For each player, write what they gain and lose in ordinary words before looking at equations. Then ask which omitted consequence would most likely reverse the comparison between two actions, and whether that consequence belongs to one player or to the designer.
what_changes_if_false: A threat can look irrational when reputation was omitted, cooperation can look impossible when future relationships were omitted, and an auction rule can look truthful when bidder risk or budget constraints were omitted.
mathematical_symptom: The symptom is a payoff inequality whose sign depends on an unstated term. If adding a cost c, future value delta V, or outside option O changes the sign, the original conclusion was assumption-sensitive.
repair_move: State the payoff boundary explicitly: this result holds if the listed payoff components are the only strategic consequences that matter. Then add a sensitivity sentence naming the most dangerous omitted term.
naive_overread: The naive overread is to treat a payoff table as if it already contains everything humans or firms care about. A payoff entry is only a compressed modeling claim. It may leave out reputation, search costs, legal risk, future access, or the platform objective that would change the behavior.
stress_test: Add one omitted term in plain language and ask whether the comparison flips. For example, add a future relationship value to a one-shot payoff, or add budget risk to an auction payoff. If the sign changes, the result is not wrong, but it is local to the simpler payoff map.
transfer_red_flag: When a paper exports a result from a clean classroom game to a market, institution, or platform, check whether the payoff definition travels too. If the new setting has reputational, dynamic, or regulatory consequences absent from the model, mark the conclusion as assumption-sensitive. A strong transfer should say why those omitted consequences are small, constant, or irrelevant to the comparison being made.
evidence_that_would_change_mind: Look for behavior that systematically contradicts the listed payoff ranking: actors paying large costs to protect reputation, refusing profitable short-run moves to keep future access, or choosing options that only make sense after adding risk or outside options. That evidence does not automatically refute the model, but it says the payoff map is missing a term that real actors treat as material.
narrow_claim_after_audit: State the result as conditional on the payoff map: given these measured consequences and no additional reputation, risk, budget, or outside-option term, this action is optimal or stable. Do not state that the actor truly prefers it in the world until the omitted pressures have been bounded. The clean claim is about the represented incentives, not the actor's full lived objective.

title: Did the model include the deviations that could break the answer?
hidden_assumption: The listed action set contains every relevant move a player could use to improve their situation inside the question being asked.
why_it_exists: Equilibrium and incentive checks only compare available deviations. A conclusion can pass because the dangerous action was never allowed into the model, not because the behavior is truly stable.
audit_test: After a proposed solution, ask every player: what would you try instead if you wanted to exploit this outcome? If that move is plausible in the real setting but absent from the model, mark the claim as incomplete and decide whether the omission is an intentional rule or an accidental shortcut.
what_changes_if_false: A Nash equilibrium may disappear after adding a missing strategy, a mechanism may stop being truthful after adding a misreport, and a bargaining result may change after adding a walk-away option.
mathematical_symptom: The symptom is a best-response or incentive-compatibility claim over a narrow set A_i. If a larger feasible set A_i' contains a profitable deviation, the original no-deviation statement no longer proves stability.
repair_move: Name the action boundary and rerun the local deviation check. If the omitted move is important but intentionally excluded, explain what institution, technology, or timing rule rules it out.
naive_overread: The naive overread is to say no one wants to deviate when the model only checked the moves it happened to list. Stability is only meaningful relative to the action menu. A missing action can make the no-deviation statement technically true and practically misleading.
stress_test: Add the most tempting omitted move and rerun the local check. In an auction, add a misreport or budget constraint. In bargaining, add delay or exit. In competition, add entry, capacity, or price discrimination. If the result changes, the action set was doing hidden work. Then ask whether an institution truly blocks the new move or whether the original model simply forgot it.
transfer_red_flag: Watch for phrases like cannot, may not, or assume away. Those often mark institutions that restrict the action set. If the real setting does not have the same restriction, the model's equilibrium or incentive claim may not transfer. The fastest practical check is to ask a domain expert what a participant would actually try if the modeled outcome hurt them.
evidence_that_would_change_mind: Look for observed deviations outside the formal action set: side payments, identity splitting, delay, renegotiation, entry, hidden quality changes, or legal workarounds. If real participants use those moves when incentives are strong, the action boundary is too narrow for the applied claim. Evidence of even rare but profitable off-menu moves matters because equilibrium only checked the menu it was given.
narrow_claim_after_audit: State the result over the modeled menu only: no listed action is a profitable deviation, or the mechanism blocks the listed misreports. Do not claim real-world stability unless the omitted moves are impossible, dominated, illegal and enforced, or irrelevant by evidence. If enforcement is the reason, name the enforcement mechanism rather than hiding it inside the word feasible.

title: Does the timing match what actors can observe before choosing?
hidden_assumption: The game form correctly states who moves first, who observes what, and whether later choices are made after earlier events are known.
why_it_exists: Timing determines credibility. A move that is attractive before an event may be unattractive after the event, and a response that requires observation cannot be chosen if the actor does not see the relevant history.
audit_test: Draw a small calendar. At each point write who chooses, what they have seen, and what they still do not know. If two events are ordered in the real story but simultaneous in the model, ask whether that compression changes incentives.
what_changes_if_false: A threat may be treated as binding when it is not, a punishment may be assumed after an unobserved deviation, or a simultaneous Nash check may be used where backward induction or subgame perfection is required.
mathematical_symptom: The symptom is a solution concept that ignores a later node or an information set. If the model needs a continuation value or subgame check but uses only a one-shot profile, the timing assumption is doing hidden work.
repair_move: Replace the flat representation with a tree when order and observation matter. Then solve from the last meaningful choice backward and state which histories are being checked.
naive_overread: The naive overread is to treat timing as presentation rather than substance. In strategic problems, the order of moves changes what can be believed, what can be punished, and which responses are available. A simultaneous table can hide a credibility problem.
stress_test: Move one action earlier or later and ask whether the best response changes. Then remove an observation and ask whether the punishment or response can still be conditioned on it. If either change affects the result, timing and observation are load-bearing assumptions. Also test commitment separately from timing, because moving first is not the same as being able to bind later behavior.
transfer_red_flag: When a paper says agents observe, commit, announce, threaten, punish, or respond, check whether the formal game gives them that timing and information. If the prose is sequential but the model is static, the compression needs justification. A good compression should explain why solving the reduced table gives the same incentives as solving the visible timeline.
evidence_that_would_change_mind: Look for delays, information lags, private observations, or commitment devices that contradict the modeled timeline. If actors choose before seeing the event that supposedly triggers their response, or if they can bind themselves before a later temptation arrives, the timing assumption must be rewritten. A contract, precommitted algorithm, or public irreversible investment can change the tree as much as a new payoff term.
narrow_claim_after_audit: State the result for the represented timing: with these observations available at these nodes, this continuation is credible or not credible. Avoid saying the threat, promise, or punishment works in general until the real calendar and information flow match the tree. The narrow claim should include who observes which history before choosing.

title: Where did the beliefs come from?
hidden_assumption: Beliefs are either given by the model, updated from observed evidence, or constrained by the strategies that would have produced the observations.
why_it_exists: Private-information games do not work if beliefs float freely. What a buyer, bidder, or receiver believes changes which action is sensible, and the observed action should usually be connected to which type would have chosen it.
audit_test: For every belief, ask whether it is a prior, a posterior after evidence, or an off-path belief. If it is a posterior, ask what likelihood comparison made it move.
what_changes_if_false: A signal may look persuasive without an imitation check, cheap talk may look informative without incentive alignment, and a Bayesian equilibrium may use beliefs that do not match the proposed strategies.
mathematical_symptom: The symptom is a posterior probability or equilibrium belief that appears without Bayes-rule support. On observed paths, posterior belief should be proportional to prior times likelihood of the observed signal under each type.
repair_move: Write the belief update in words before symbols: this observation is more likely under type H than type L, so belief in H rises. If the observation is off path, mark the belief as an assumption and test whether the result depends on it.
naive_overread: The naive overread is to treat beliefs as flexible explanations for whatever behavior the model wants. In a disciplined private-information model, beliefs are part of the mechanism: they come from priors, signals, strategies, or explicit off-path assumptions.
stress_test: Change the prior, alter the likelihood of the signal under each type, or let an imitator type send the same signal. Then ask whether the posterior and chosen action still move the same way. If the result flips, the belief source is carrying the conclusion. For off-path behavior, try two plausible beliefs and see whether the equilibrium survives both.
transfer_red_flag: Look for belief statements that appear after the equilibrium is announced. If a paper does not say how the receiver got the belief, or whether the belief is on path or off path, treat the information argument as incomplete until that source is named. The audit should also ask whether the same observed action could have been sent by an imitator type. If imitation is easy, the belief update needs more than the observed action itself.
evidence_that_would_change_mind: Look for pooling behavior, frequent imitation, unstable priors, or signals sent by types the model says should not send them. Those observations weaken the belief update because the same evidence no longer points strongly toward one hidden type. Also watch whether receivers actually behave as if the posterior changed; ignored signals are evidence against the modeled belief channel.
narrow_claim_after_audit: State belief conclusions as conditional on the prior, likelihoods, and strategy profile. Say the signal raises belief in a type under these assumptions, not that it proves the type. Off-path beliefs should be labeled as assumptions, not transcript-backed or data-backed facts. The claim is about disciplined belief movement, not certain revelation.

title: Can players actually observe and punish the behavior?
hidden_assumption: The repeated-game punishment can be triggered by observable behavior, and the punishment path is itself credible when it starts.
why_it_exists: Future punishment disciplines present temptation only if players can detect enough about the deviation and will actually want to carry out the punishment afterward. The future cannot threaten the present if nobody can tell whether the triggering event happened.
audit_test: Ask what the deviator gains today, what signal reveals the deviation, what punishment follows, and why the punishers will not abandon the punishment when the future arrives. Then ask whether a false alarm would punish an innocent player.
what_changes_if_false: Cooperation can collapse if cheating is hidden, noisy signals create mistaken punishment, or the punishment hurts the punisher so much that it is not credible. The same discount factor can support cooperation under clear monitoring and fail under noisy monitoring.
mathematical_symptom: The symptom is a discounting inequality that includes a punishment value without proving the punishment can be triggered and sustained. The continuation value must be feasible under the information and incentives of the repeated game.
repair_move: Add the monitoring assumption and the punishment credibility check beside the discount-factor calculation. If monitoring is imperfect, weaken the claim or mark it as requiring a richer repeated-game model.
naive_overread: The naive overread is to say future punishment supports cooperation because the relationship repeats. Repetition only matters if deviation is detected, punishment is triggered, and carrying out punishment remains rational when the future arrives.
stress_test: Introduce noisy monitoring or delayed observation. Ask whether players can tell cheating from bad luck, and whether the proposed punishment would punish the wrong person too often. Then check whether the punishment path is still a best response for the punishers. If punishment is costly to carry out, rerun the continuation check from the punisher's later point of view.
transfer_red_flag: In applications to cartels, platforms, or relationships, watch for claims that rely on retaliation without showing what signal reveals the deviation. If the monitoring technology is vague, the repeated-game conclusion is not yet earned. Also ask whether punishment is legal, affordable, and distinguishable from ordinary competitive response in the real setting. If punishment cannot be separated from market noise, the model needs a noise-aware version.
evidence_that_would_change_mind: Look for undetected cheating, false punishment after bad luck, punishment that quickly stops because it is too costly, or noisy public signals that cannot identify the deviator. Those patterns show that the continuation path is not available in the clean way the inequality assumes. If participants keep cooperating despite noisy signals, the model may need trust, communication, or institutional enforcement beyond trigger punishment.
narrow_claim_after_audit: State cooperation as sustainable only under the specified monitoring and punishment technology. The safe claim is not that repetition sustains cooperation, but that clear detection plus credible continuation losses can sustain it when the discount factor is high enough. Include the detection condition beside the patience condition because both are required.

title: Which auction assumptions make the theorem work?
hidden_assumption: The bidders, values, risk attitudes, allocation rule, payment rule, and information environment match the conditions needed for the auction result.
why_it_exists: Auction results often look broader than they are because the format labels are familiar. Revenue equivalence, truthful bidding, and ad-auction ranking claims rely on specific assumptions about values, reports, and incentives. The theorem lives in the environment, not in the word auction.
audit_test: Ask whether values are private or common, whether bidders are symmetric, whether bidders are risk neutral, whether budgets matter, and whether the same bidder type receives the object with the same probability across formats. Then ask which of those answers the lecture theorem needed.
what_changes_if_false: Revenue equivalence can fail, truthful reporting can stop being attractive, and a ranking rule that appears efficient can distort incentives once quality scores, budgets, or correlated values matter.
mathematical_symptom: The symptom is an expected-payment or incentive-compatibility result that skips the environment. If the allocation probability, lowest-type payoff, or deviation set changes, expected payments need not remain equivalent.
repair_move: State the auction environment before comparing formats. Then separate the allocation rule from the payment rule and identify which assumption would change the bidder's expected payoff comparison first. If the environment differs, downgrade the theorem to an analogy or rebuild the incentive comparison.
naive_overread: The naive overread is to think an auction theorem belongs to the auction label. The theorem usually belongs to a precise environment: private values, symmetry, risk neutrality, independent signals, a given allocation rule, and a particular payment rule.
stress_test: Change one environmental feature at a time: make bidders risk averse, add budgets, correlate values, add reserve prices, or alter quality scoring. Then ask whether the same allocation probabilities and payment comparisons survive. This reveals which assumption actually powers the theorem. If expected revenue changes, trace whether the cause was allocation, payment, entry, risk, or information.
transfer_red_flag: When a paper moves from textbook auctions to ad auctions, procurement, platforms, or data markets, check whether values, budgets, quality scores, and repeated participation still match the theorem assumptions. Familiar auction vocabulary is not enough. The audit should identify the first theorem assumption that fails before using the theorem as guidance. That failed assumption should determine which calculation gets rebuilt first.
evidence_that_would_change_mind: Look for bidder budgets binding, correlated values, risk aversion, endogenous entry, quality-score manipulation, or repeated learning across auctions. Any of those patterns can move the allocation probability, payment rule, or deviation incentives away from the theorem environment. Field evidence that bidders shade differently across formats is a warning that revenue equivalence or truthfulness assumptions are not traveling.
narrow_claim_after_audit: State the auction theorem inside its environment: with this value structure, risk attitude, allocation rule, payment rule, and information condition, the result follows. For ad auctions or platforms, call it an analogy until the actual expected payoff comparison is rebuilt. The narrow applied claim should name which theorem assumptions survived the move.

title: Is the message public, private, credible, or just cheap talk?
hidden_assumption: The model correctly distinguishes a public signal from separate private signals, and it does not treat costless words as automatically informative.
why_it_exists: Information changes strategic behavior through what people know about what others know. Communication also depends on incentives: a sender may want the receiver to believe something even when it is not true. Publicness and credibility are separate assumptions.
audit_test: Ask who hears the message, whether everyone knows who heard it, whether the sender pays a cost for lying, and whether sender and receiver interests are aligned enough for the message to carry information. Then separate shared awareness from truthful content.
what_changes_if_false: A coordination result can fail if the signal is private rather than public. A cheap-talk result can fail if the sender's incentives point away from truthful communication.
mathematical_symptom: The symptom is a common-knowledge or cheap-talk claim that treats information as a fact transfer only. The missing object is higher-order belief or an incentive comparison for the sender's message.
repair_move: Mark the message type explicitly: public announcement, private signal, costly signal, or cheap talk. Then test whether behavior relies on shared awareness, belief updating, or incentive-aligned communication. If two roles are mixed, split them before applying common-knowledge or signaling logic.
naive_overread: The naive overread is to treat all information as data transfer. In games, a message can coordinate, reveal, mislead, or merely repeat a fact publicly. Those functions require different assumptions about who hears it and why the sender would say it.
stress_test: Turn a public message into separate private messages and ask whether coordination still works. Then make the message costless and ask whether the sender would still tell the truth. If either change breaks the result, publicness or incentive alignment was doing real work. Next reverse the test: make a cheap message public and ask whether publicness alone fixes the sender's incentive problem.
transfer_red_flag: Watch for papers that move between signaling, cheap talk, and common knowledge without changing the assumptions. A costly signal, a cheap message, and a public announcement are not interchangeable even when the sentence communicated is the same. The audit should ask whether the result needs credibility, publicness, or both. If it needs both, each must be justified separately.
evidence_that_would_change_mind: Look for receivers ignoring messages, senders using the same message in all states, audiences receiving different versions, or public announcements interpreted differently across groups. Those observations tell you whether the failure is credibility, publicness, shared meaning, or all three. If behavior changes only after the message becomes public, publicness rather than factual content is probably doing the work.
narrow_claim_after_audit: State communication results by message type: this is a publicness result, an incentive-alignment result, or a costly-signal result. Do not say information changes behavior until the mechanism specifies who heard it, why they believed it, and whether others know they heard it. If the result needs both truthfulness and publicness, claim both assumptions explicitly.
